docs.title: Why do we need to color sort?
docs.text:
Our bot's scoring and storage mechanism is 2 chambers. We chose to use 2 chambers because it has a few advantages over a regular, single chamber lever bot. One of these benefits is simply more storage space. The other main benefit, however, excites me more; having 2 separate chambers allows us to separate the red blocks from the blue blocks.

Any bot without a color sorting mechanism runs the risk of scoring points for the opponent and their options are limited to: avoid the wrong color as much as possible, carefully try to score their own color while trying to remove the opposing color, or just give up and score the opponent some points.

A bot with a color sorting system can simply pick up blocks and not worry about the bad ones. This saves a lot of time and does not score points for the opponent.

Not all lever bot designs that want to color sort need 2 barrels! In fact, I have not seen a single lever bot with 2 barrels, but I have seen plenty that can color sort. Most bots, lever or otherwise, simply eject the wrong color during or just after intaking. We considered this as well. Ignoring the benefit of increased storage, there is still another advantage our double chamber has over regular color sorting; The ability to keep the opposite color.

Why would we want to keep the wrong color? Perhaps we want to stop the other team from getting more blocks? No, It is too hard to monopolize blocks, too easy to descore, and 5-7 blocks wouldn't make much of a difference. Perhaps we want to use them to strategically position our blocks in the control zones? No, a single lever design that could adjust the block lineup would be better suited for that. Besides, that gives points to the other side, it is just as easy to pick up more of our own blocks. There appears to be no logical reason to want to hold on to your opponent's blocks in match! That is because there is not a good enough reason in a match to justify a double chamber design. The reason comes not from a match, but from the skills challenge.

This is the is scoring for the skills challenge:

Category Points Each Block Scored in a Goal 1 Point Each filled Control Zone in a Long Goal 5 Points Each filled Control Zone in a Center Goal 10 Points Each Cleared Park Zone 5 Points Each Cleared Loader 5 Points Parked Robot 15 Points There is 2 long goals and 2 center goals. That is 30 points for just the goals (not including the points for the individual blocks). The rule book explains these 2 categories as follows:

"A Control Zone is considered filled if it ends the Match containing its maximum number of Scored Blocks, and if all Blocks in that Control Zone are the same color (e.g., all are blue, or all are red). - i. In a Robot Skills Match, a Center Goal Control Zone must contain at least seven (7) Blocks to be considered filled. - ii. A Long Goal must include one or more of the following to be considered filled in a Robot Skills Match: 1. Three Blocks of the same color fully contained between the inner edges of the Control Zone tape lines. 2. Four Blocks of the same color fully contained between the outer edges of the Control Zone tape lines."

This means that in order to get these 30 points from control zones, all blocks in the control zone needs to be the same color. For a bot without color sorting, these 30 points are very difficult to get. With a regular color sorting bot, it becomes a little easier. But with our bot separates and keeps both colors, making this much easier. This allows us to in theory get very good skills scores, both autonomous and driver control.

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: A PTO is a "power take off" where you have some sort of mechanism/gearshift that switches a motor between two (or more applications)

docs.title: Why do we need a PTO?
docs.text:
In our last bot we were very fast, to achieve that (without overheating) we needed a 6 motor drive, this was very limiting on the other mechanisms on our bot because we only had 2 more motors we could use.

A PTO can help solve this problem; we don't always need the torque of all 6 motors, so when we don't need them on the drive train we can switch 2 motor off and use them in other mechanisms. This would be especially useful for mechanism's that could use energy stored in elastics/similar (ex. like theorized in Linear Scoring)

Timeline of PTO: Use stored energy is used --> PTO switches 2 motors off the drive train --> those 2 motors wind up the stored energy --> the energy is used --> repeat.

Even if we aren't going to store energy is is still very viable

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
How would we actuality accomplish this? There are 2 main ways of implementing a PTO:

Vertically: This method rotates the motor gear around a pivot point to mesh with a top or bottom gear: Image Credit

Horizontally: This method slides the motor gear along a shaft and slides to the teeth of one gear or another, I can't find a very good example of this method for a PTO but this one is a transmission and the concept is the same:

Image Credit: I can't' find where I got this from...

This particular one uses two "fingers" to move the gears side to side and engage different gears.

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Very fast switching
  • Relatively simple

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• If enough pressure isn't applied it can skip teeth under high load
  • Requires a lot of vertical space

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Loses no torque
  • Very reliable when tuned

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Not super fast switching
  • A bit more complicated
  • More friction

docs.text:
I am going to select the horizontal method because the chance of running out of air is not worth it to me, because if we ran out of air for the vertical method, we wouldn't be able to use it in ether application (drivetrain/other).

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
We need more traction and torque, mostly traction, as we cant really change torque as the speed is set in mostly dry clay.

Because speed (and torque is set) we need other solutions to help with pushing/being pushed. Something that could help is adding angled skirts to edge of the drivetrain

As shown in this diagram, if we have a slope on the edge of our bot if another bot tries to push us it would get lifted up losing the majority of its traction This also helps with pushing other bots, because when we go push someone else it will lift them up a little bit , making them lose their traction and pushing us into the ground giving us more traction (we might have a little bit of a hard time with traction because we are planning on making our robot light)

There is a problem with this however; to be most effective the skirts bust be close to the ground, and that will make it difficult to park, so we need a way to raise up the skirt, and if we add that ability, we might as well make it so we can push it into the ground making effectively immovable ~~This can also help with Parking; we could make it the same mechanism.~~ Better solutions in Aligner

docs.title: Legality:
docs.text:
Rule GG17 states that a Robot may not Hold an opposing Robot for more than a 3-count during the Driver Controlled Period.

Holding is defined as:

Holding - A Robot status; see rule < GG17 > for more information. Holding is legal until it exceeds the limits in < GG17 >. A Robot is considered to be Holding if it meets any of the following criteria during a Match: - Trapping - Limiting the movement of an opponent Robot to a small or confined area of the Field, approximately the size of one foam field tile or less, without an avenue for escape. Note that if a Robot is not attempting to escape, it is not considered Trapped. - Pinning - Preventing the movement of an opponent Robot through contact with the Field Perimeter, a Field Element, or another Robot. - Lifting - Controlling an opponent’s movements by raising or tilting the opponent’s Robot off of the foam tiles. Preventing a Robot that is already off of the Floor from returning to the Floor may also be considered Lifting or Trapping.

It is also mentioned that "Holding is a standard and legal part of Head-to-Head game play, and only becomes a Violation if it exceeds the guidelines in this rule. By beginning a Holding count immediately after noticing a Holding interaction, and providing a visual signal when a Holding interaction has been cleared, Head Referees can help Teams avoid penalties."

Therefore if we were to use a skirt/wedge to lift another robot it would just be considered Holding and is not directly illegal.

Daren 12/8/25, 12/14/25

docs.title: Screw Joints
docs.text: Screw joints are a very common technique for reducing friction. The method of screw joints (on a drivetrain) is to connect a gear and a wheel together with screws like so: We do this so that we can use round inserts on the wheel but still be able to turn it (cuz we kinda need to drive). Using the round inserts allows us to use a screw instead of a axle witch is smoother and produces less friction.

docs.title: Inserts
docs.text:
Building upon the idea of screw joints, the type of round insert matters. The best inserts are the round bronze inserts, these have a lot less friction than the plastic ones because they are smoother and are "gripped" less easily by the screw threads (when a lot of force is applied perpendicular to the screw, the threads can "cut" into the plastic and that creates a lot of friction) This is an example of how good the bronze inserts are:

Your browser does not support the video tag.

docs.title: Bearings
docs.text: Never put an axle on bare metal, even if the hole is round, it will wear down both the metal and the axle.

docs.title: Lubricant
docs.text: Some mechanisms benefit from lubrication to reduce friction and wear. A good rule of thumb: if a part squeaks, binds, or shows wear (like powder from plastic gears), it may need grease. For VEX parts, white lithium grease is safe and effective for metal and plastic (acetal) components. Apply sparingly (ahem.. Zack... ahem....).

docs.title: No Bent stuff
docs.text: Don't use bent parts (especially turney things).

docs.title: Don't use them.

Our old bot uses rubber bands on large sprockets to intake blocks. It was in a fixed position; it doesn't move up and down to let blocks in, the rubber bands just deform around the block. 

TODO: find where to put this
For the new intake we are thinking of either sticking with the rubber band intake, or switching to a flex wheel intake. a flex wheel intake is harder to make, as it has tighter tolerances of actually working, where rubber band intake requires almost no tuning. lets list out all the pros and cons

docs.title: Rubber band intake
docs.text: This intake type uses sprockets and rubber bands to make a spinning drum that intakes the blocks.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Simple
  • Little required tuning
  • Can be static (not move up and down)
  • Doesn't rely solely on friction, the gaps in the rubber bands act as little "slots" for the blocks to go into.

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Tangles with other robots easily
  • Rubber bands break and it goes through a lot of them
  • Jams if not done right (block can get stuck against the sprockets)

docs.title: Flex wheel intake
docs.text: This intake type uses a line of flex-wheels to grip the blocks and intake them Credit

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• No constant replacements needed
  • Generally smaller than a rubber band intake
  • Harder to jam

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Once the flex wheels get dirty/dusty it barely works
  • Need to be mounted on a pivot (move up and down)

docs.title: Chain flap intake
docs.text: This intake method uses sprockets with rubber-flap chains like so:

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Doesn't need replacing
  • Doesn't matter if it is dirty (doesn't rely on friction to much)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Not as affective as rubber band or flex wheel intakes (when they are working well)
  • It is "floppy"
  • To be effective it needs to be big

docs.title: Match Loader
docs.text: plastic match loader mech

docs.title: Problems with Old Scoring (and Intake):
docs.text:
Our past bot used rollers to pull blocks from the basket and score them. This method worked decently well and was able to move a lot of blocks pretty quickly. But had some issues:

  1. Rubber band entanglement - The intake (and output) relied on rubber bands, which were really good at intaking but would get entangled with other bots. This would either:
    • Break the rubber bands completely
    • Make our bot stuck to the opponent for the rest of the match
  2. Jamming when overheated - The system would jam if the motors got too hot during extended use
  3. Size - The system was almost or more than half the bot and we couldn't fit under the goal
  4. Middle/Bottom goal - The old system could barely score in the middle goal if at all, and could only really score one block at a time in the bottom goal.

docs.title: What Worked Well:
docs.text:
• Fast block movement
  • Effective intake (when not entangled)
  • Generally consistent performance under normal conditions

docs.title: Goals for New Scoring System:
docs.text:
• Extremely fast scoring capability
  • More reliable (jamming)
  • No overheating issues under full match load
  • Ability to score specific quantities of blocks (important for autonomous)
  • Color sorting capability for strategic play
  • Fit under long goal

docs.title: Research - Current Meta:
docs.text:
Looking at top-performing bots at competitions, we've identified several effective scoring mechanisms:

  1. Basket - What we used before, moderate speed
  2. Lever - Currently the fastest method (6 blocks in ~0.5 seconds)
  3. S-bot -
  4. C-bot -

docs.title: Dual-Chamber Idea:
docs.text: Regardless of which mechanism we choose, we're considering using 2 scoring chambers side-by-side that converge into one output point. But there are multiple way to push the blocks: - Arc Scoring - Linear Scoring

docs.title: Potential Advantages:
docs.text:
• ~12 block capacity (double the standard 6)
  • Color sorting - one color per chamber
  • Strategic flexibility - can score from either chamber independently
  • Redundancy - if one jams, we can still use the other
  • Very fast - SPEED

docs.title: Scoring Methods Under Consideration:
docs.text:
1. Arc Scoring - Arc/lever mechanism analysis
  2. Linear Scoring - Linear elastic-powered system
  3. S Scoring - S-shaped path variation
  4. C Scoring - C-shaped path variation

docs.title: Select:
docs.text: Based on the ideas discussed in the above sections; the best option looks to be an Arc-Scoring lever as it: - Utilizes the PTO more effectively than linear options - Can fit 12 blocks (double standard capacity with dual chamber) - Doesn't have cooldown between uses.

docs.title: Implementation:
docs.text:
Arc-Scoring Implementation

  Zach 12/10/2025-12/12/2025 
  Daren 12/10/2025-12/12/2025, 1/7/2026

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: We have a lot of the same constraints as the section of the scoring method

docs.title: Goals:
docs.text:
• Fast (0.5 sec)
  • Reliable (no jamming)
  • No overheating issues under full match load
  • Score specific quantities of blocks (important for autonomous)
  • Color sorting
  • Fit under long goal
  • ~~Hold 12 blocks (6 in each chamber)~~ Hold 10 blocks (5 in each chamber) (other constraints)
  • Lightweight

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
To actually make this we need to layout how it is going to work I have made a little diagram to visualize how i think this will go:

We need to plan out a few mechanisms: - The lever chamber(s) - The lever(s) (the thing that actually pushes the blocks) - Chamber height (long vs mid goal height) - Integration with the intake/color sorting - Integration with the PTO

docs.title: Relevant constraints:
docs.text:
• Hold 12 blocks
  • Fit under long goal
  • Reliability
  • Lightweight

docs.title: Size and shape
docs.text: In order for us to fit 6 (12 total) in a chamber we will want to look at how much liner space we need: A block has a maximum size of ~4 inches if we plan for worst case we would need (6*4=) 24 inches of chamber (worst case) If we look at the smallest distance (3.25 inches) we will need a minimum of 19.5 inches. Therefore, to fit 6 blocks we need the chamber(s) to have a 19.5-24 inch path length I drew out the design with some constraints, and there is a little problem: With the current constraints the easiest spot for the chambers to go is not long enough (understatement). With a path length of 17 inches the most blocks we could fit would be ~5.2 blocks which is useable.

docs.title: Chamber height
docs.text: We need to think about how we are going to change heights as we think about size. The most common (and easiest) way to do this is a four bar lift to switch between the long and mid goal:

docs.title: Levers
docs.text:
We need a way to push the blocks out the front of the lever. My first idea is to use a pivoting c-channel (commonly used for lever bots) like this: It pivots up and pushes the blocks There is a little problem with this; the position of where it would need to pivot is really far forward and the way the PTO is setup right now is not ideal for this: It would be ideal to just use this pivot point, and i have an idea on how to do so. 4-bar lever: A 4-bar lift that has the horizontal bars attached on opposite sides to allow 180° of motion with a pushing "head" that stays facing one direction at all times. This has a great advantage as it lets us put the pivot point in the middle of the chamber as opposed to the front of the chamber. With this exact mechanism has a few problems with the angle of how it pushes the blocks (it would likely get stuck). A solution to this is to use a trapezoidal four-bar linkage instead of a normal 2 bar linkage where the top and bottom links are different lengths. this causes the angle of the "head" to rotate as it pivots. After messing around with different spacing i found one that works really well:

With this motion the blocks shouldn't get stuck as easily

docs.text: Daren 1/7/2026

docs.title: Arc Scoring
docs.text: Arc scoring is using a lever to push blocks along an arc-shaped path and into the goals.

docs.title: How It Works:
docs.text: The way this would work is by using a PTO (Power Take Off) to switch 2 of the drivetrain motors to the lever(s), and rotate them along the arc, which would be full of blocks. This method has been proven to be able to score 6 blocks in 1/2 a second. This method of scoring is also known to jam a lot if it's not built properly.

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Is extremely fast
  • Can score a specific amount of blocks (1, 2, 3, etc.) - this is important for things like autonomous period and skills autonomous, when you want to only score one or 2 blocks, and not everything you are holding
  • Can have variable speed, in case you want to launch the blocks really hard and fast to either de-score, or try and win a pushing match where there's 2 bots on opposing ends of goals just holding it, or if you want to score slowly to not shoot them through the middle goal
  • Very lightweight

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Can be weak if it's not built for torque
  • Takes up more room than linear (harder to go under goals)
  • Can have issues with intaking if not built correctly
  • 4 motor drive while scoring

docs.title: Conclusion:
docs.text:
I think this is the better method of scoring due to the fact that linear isn't adjustable. Like it can't vary the speed, or the amount of blocks it scores, it's all or nothing. With the lever arm, you can do just about anything in terms of scoring. You can make it super slow to score, or you can make it launch the blocks out the other side of the long goal.

For auton, you can score one or two in the middle, and the rest in the long goal. Or if you want to get AWP, you can score 1 in the middle goal, go to match loader and score 2 in the long goal, then go to the other match loader and score all 6 into the other long goal, and use a wing to get control zone. This gives an insane head start to the rest of the match, with us already owning one goal.

Zach/Daren 12/10/2025-12/12/2025

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
One way to score blocks is using a linear mechanism to push the blocks. My idea is a little difficult to describe in words so here is a diagram:

In the block chamber we have a liner rail and slide and on that slide we have something to push the blocks out the end. The slide would have elastic string attached to it that would be wound up by the PTO.

There would be 3 main states:

State 1: In this state there is no tension on the elastic string or the block pusher thingy, but the latch holds the block pusher thingy from going forward.

State 2: State 2 is vary similar to state 2 except that the PTO has wound up the elastic string and stored the energy to be released by the latch

State 3: State 3 is the same as state 2 but after the latch has been released but the string is still wound up.

After state 3 the PTO unwinds the elastic string and a small elastic pulls the slide back into the latch resetting to state 1

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Doesn't take up a lot of additional space
  • Doesn't require a motor to actively use (to score blocks)
  • Can release a lot more energy at once than a motor directly (it just takes time to wind up, the limit isn't torque it's time)
  • Is extremely fast at scoring
  • can be very lightweight

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Less efficient block storage (not curved)
  • A bit complicated (ok, maybe a lot)
  • Not super controllable
  • Requires the PTO to be engaged in winding mode for much longer time than other methods would require

  • difficult (if not impossible) to score less than all of the blocks in the chamber

    Daren 12/09/25
